p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> As the debate about taxing billionaires to fund healthcare escalates, California voters also will face decisions about whether to approve two propositions that could cancel out the proposed wealth tax.
Those measures include Proposition 41, also known as the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act.
Supporters say the measure aims to cut wasteful government spending by requiring audits for new state special taxes. It also would bar new state taxes that exempt their revenue from a state spending limit. Since this conflicts with the proposed wealth tax, opponents say it’s a “billionaire-funded smoke screen” that would block the billionaire tax.

What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 41 requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot. The auditor would examine whether the program is achieving its goals, how to cut the program’s costs by at least 10% annually and other areas. Under the act, new or higher special taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, would be audited every four years.
The act also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit. That could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. This could happen if Proposition 41 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40.
How much they have raised
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text">
Fundraising data will be updated regularly until the election.
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The California Taxpayers Assn., the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, the CalAsian Chamber of Commerce and others back the proposition. They say it would result in the government spending taxpayer dollars more wisely while improving transparency.
The bulk of the contributions to support the proposition have come from Building a Better California, data from the California secretary of state’s website show. Top contributors to Building a Better California include Sergey Brin, Google’s co-founder; John Doerr, chairman of venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins; and Eric Schmidt, the former chief executive of Google.
Advertisement
Proposition 41 “requires more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes,” a website for the proposition states.
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the group behind the proposed billionaire tax, opposes Proposition 41.
In arguments against the measure, SEIU-UHW Chief of Staff Suzanne Jimenez wrote that the billionaires don’t care about government accountability and have been avoiding higher taxes through loopholes and tax breaks.
“This sham initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce,” Jimenez wrote.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The proposition states its purpose is to make sure that “programs are delivering results, and that taxpayer dollars are not being lost to inefficiency, waste or abuse.” Opponents say the proposition is meant to nullify the proposed billionaire tax.

‘Billionaire tax’ Prop 40 and its rival props 41 and 42
We dive deep into Prop 40 and its rival props, 41 and 42, and what's at stake.
Proposition 41 would make it harder to pass new special taxes in California. It would require the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters, and it would count any new special tax that voters approve toward the state’s spending cap.
Opponents of Prop. 40, the proposed “billionaire tax,” (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-prop-40-billionaire-tax) placed this measure on the ballot.
What’s at stake
This measure would make it more difficult to raise taxes in the future.
Here’s how it would work: If successful, Prop. 41 would require the state auditor to assess any proposed new taxes. Before any public vote, the auditor would identify ways the program set to benefit from the tax increase could cut its spending by at least 10% each year. A summary of this audit would appear in the information guide that’s mailed to voters. Prop. 41 would also require new special taxes to count toward California’s spending cap.
Prop. 41 directly undermines Prop. 40 (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-prop-40-billionaire-tax), the proposed wealth tax on billionaires, which exempts its potential revenue from the spending cap. Both Prop. 41 and Prop. 42 (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-proposition-42) were backed by Building a Better California (https://www.buildingabetterca.org/), funded heavily by Google co-founder Sergey Brin. If either measure gets more votes than Prop. 40, Prop. 40 is canceled, even if it also passes.
Official title on the ballot: Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/index.htm) :
Nullifies state taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes.
What your vote means
A “yes” vote means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
A “no” vote means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
Understanding Prop. 41
Prop. 41 targets special taxes, which raise revenue for a specific purpose, such as infrastructure or healthcare.
If passed, Prop. 41 would prohibit new special taxes from exempting their revenue from the state’s spending limit, established by a 1979 ballot measure. Critics say such exemptions are a way to pour more tax money into state coffers while sidestepping the “Gann Limit.” (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-3-2026-general-election/proposition-41-audits) The Gann Limit is named after Paul Gann, an anti-tax activist, and it seeks to cap the amount of money the state can spend. (Its baseline is state spending in 1978-79 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/what-would-proposition-41-mean-for-california/), adjusted for inflation and population changes.) Whenever state revenues exceed this cap for two consecutive years, California must refund the excess directly to taxpayers and through education spending. This has only happened twice (https://apnews.com/article/california-health-coronavirus-pandemic-business-personal-taxes-228c115a231bcc8ec000c7445e83d8e7).
Watch the ballot cram session analysis
What supporters say
Supporters say key social programs aren’t getting enough money despite California’s high taxes. They argue the state auditor check would ensure programs that benefit from special taxes spend money wisely. They also want these taxes to count toward the state spending limit, which would make tax rebates to Californians more likely.
Notable supporters: Reform California, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu and Stewart Resnick, chairman and CEO of the Wonderful Company.
What opponents say
The chief opponent is SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, which sponsors Prop. 40. The union argues that Prop. 41 is designed to trick voters into blocking a wealth tax on billionaires without realizing it. It says the measure isn’t really about auditing waste in public programs, but is instead a way for billionaires to avoid paying a one-time tax on their wealth.
Notable opponents: SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the California Democratic Party, California State PTA and the American Civil Liberties Union of Southern California
Fiscal impact
If passed, Prop. 41 would increase costs for the state auditor. But those costs would depend on how many new special taxes are proposed and approved, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), which estimates these costs would likely start in the low millions of dollars per year and would grow over time.
Adding audit summaries to voter guides would increase printing and mailing costs by “a few hundred thousand dollars” per initiative, according to that same analysis. That breakdown also adds that Prop. 41 could bring savings by requiring the state auditor to recommend ways that programs can cut costs, although those savings “would depend on future decisions and are not known.”
Overall, the Legislative Analyst’s Office determined that the “net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers.”

We dive deep into Prop 40 and its rival props, 41 and 42, and what's at stake.
Proposition 41 would make it harder to pass new special taxes in California. It would require the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters, and it would count any new special tax that voters approve toward the state’s spending cap.
Opponents of Prop. 40, the proposed “billionaire tax,” (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-prop-40-billionaire-tax) placed this measure on the ballot.
What’s at stake
This measure would make it more difficult to raise taxes in the future.
Here’s how it would work: If successful, Prop. 41 would require the state auditor to assess any proposed new taxes. Before any public vote, the auditor would identify ways the program set to benefit from the tax increase could cut its spending by at least 10% each year. A summary of this audit would appear in the information guide that’s mailed to voters. Prop. 41 would also require new special taxes to count toward California’s spending cap.
Prop. 41 directly undermines Prop. 40 (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-prop-40-billionaire-tax), the proposed wealth tax on billionaires, which exempts its potential revenue from the spending cap. Both Prop. 41 and Prop. 42 (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-proposition-42) were backed by Building a Better California (https://www.buildingabetterca.org/), funded heavily by Google co-founder Sergey Brin. If either measure gets more votes than Prop. 40, Prop. 40 is canceled, even if it also passes.
Official title on the ballot: Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/index.htm) :
Nullifies state taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes.
What your vote means
A “yes” vote means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
A “no” vote means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
Understanding Prop. 41
Prop. 41 targets special taxes, which raise revenue for a specific purpose, such as infrastructure or healthcare.
If passed, Prop. 41 would prohibit new special taxes from exempting their revenue from the state’s spending limit, established by a 1979 ballot measure. Critics say such exemptions are a way to pour more tax money into state coffers while sidestepping the “Gann Limit.” (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-3-2026-general-election/proposition-41-audits) The Gann Limit is named after Paul Gann, an anti-tax activist, and it seeks to cap the amount of money the state can spend. (Its baseline is state spending in 1978-79 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/what-would-proposition-41-mean-for-california/), adjusted for inflation and population changes.) Whenever state revenues exceed this cap for two consecutive years, California must refund the excess directly to taxpayers and through education spending. This has only happened twice (https://apnews.com/article/california-health-coronavirus-pandemic-business-personal-taxes-228c115a231bcc8ec000c7445e83d8e7).
Watch the ballot cram session analysis
What supporters say
Supporters say key social programs aren’t getting enough money despite California’s high taxes. They argue the state auditor check would ensure programs that benefit from special taxes spend money wisely. They also want these taxes to count toward the state spending limit, which would make tax rebates to Californians more likely.
Notable supporters: Reform California, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu and Stewart Resnick, chairman and CEO of the Wonderful Company.
What opponents say
The chief opponent is SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, which sponsors Prop. 40. The union argues that Prop. 41 is designed to trick voters into blocking a wealth tax on billionaires without realizing it. It says the measure isn’t really about auditing waste in public programs, but is instead a way for billionaires to avoid paying a one-time tax on their wealth.
Notable opponents: SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the California Democratic Party, California State PTA and the American Civil Liberties Union of Southern California
Fiscal impact
If passed, Prop. 41 would increase costs for the state auditor. But those costs would depend on how many new special taxes are proposed and approved, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), which estimates these costs would likely start in the low millions of dollars per year and would grow over time.
Adding audit summaries to voter guides would increase printing and mailing costs by “a few hundred thousand dollars” per initiative, according to that same analysis. That breakdown also adds that Prop. 41 could bring savings by requiring the state auditor to recommend ways that programs can cut costs, although those savings “would depend on future decisions and are not known.”
Overall, the Legislative Analyst’s Office determined that the “net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers.”

Prop 40 guide: Why ‘yes’ or ‘no’ depends on two other California propositions
By Kathleen Pender (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/kathleen-pender/) , Contributor Updated Oct 31, 2026 1:33 p.m.
From left, California insurance commissioner candidate Jane Kim, Sen. Bernie Sanders, independent-Vt., and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., stand together onstage after the “Ballots Over Billionaires” wealth tax rally at the Curran Theatre in San Francisco.
Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle
Many Californians have strong opinions about Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php), the proposed “wealth tax” on billionaires. But voting for — or against — this high-stakes ballot measure in November is not as simple as voting for — or against — Prop 40.
That’s because Props 41 and 42, which never mention billionaires but are backed by some of the state’s wealthiest residents, are also on the ballot and have provisions that conflict with Prop 40. (Props 41 and 42 do not conflict with each other.)

Under the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-10/), if two conflicting measures on the same ballot both pass with more than 50% of the vote, the one that gets the most “yes” votes prevails.
The graphic below shows the possible outcomes for which propositions could take effect, depending on how the votes come in. Voters can also use it to understand the cumulative impact of how they vote on each proposition.
What it means to vote ‘yes’ or ‘no’ on Props 40, 41 and 42
Prop 40, the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, would impose a one-time “wealth tax” on the net worth of people who were California residents as of Jan. 1, 2026 — even if they later became non-residents — and had more than $1 billion in net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. It also would exempt billionaire-tax revenues from three state-spending rules, including one known as the Gann limit.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 41 would conflict with Prop 40 because it would outlaw new taxes passed after Jan. 1, 2026 that are exempt from the Gann limit. Prop 42 also appears to counter Prop 40 by preventing new taxes on personal property (i.e., wealth) and taxes that apply retroactively, including those based on residency.
Backers of the billionaire tax are urging people (https://yeson40.com/) to vote “Yes” on 40 and “No” on Props 41 and 42. If voters follow that advice or, vote the exact opposite way, the outcomes would be straightforward:
If Prop 40 passes with more than 50% of the vote and Prop 41 and Prop 42 do not: The billionaire tax would take effect and the other two would not.
If Prop 40 loses and Prop 41 and/or 42 pass: The billionaire tax would fail. Prop 41 would take effect if it got a simple majority. So would Prop 42 if it passed.
But what happens if Prop 40 gets more than half the vote, and so does Prop 41 and/or 42? Here is the conventional wisdom:
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 41 passes with more votes than Prop 40: Prop 41 takes effect and the billionaire does not.
Prop 42 passes with more votes than Prop 40: Prop 42 takes effect, the billionaire tax dies.
Prop 40 passes with more votes than Prop 41: Prop 40 gets enacted, Prop 41 is invalidated.
Prop 40 passes with more votes than Prop 42: Prop 40 takes effect, and cancels out Prop 42.
Although these are likely scenarios, anything could happen in a court of law. The losing side could argue that its proposition doesn’t conflict with the winning one, so they should both take effect. A court would have to decide if they do conflict.
The losing side also might argue that some parts of its measure do not conflict with the winning proposition — and those parts should take effect. The California Supreme Court has rejected this piecemeal approach, but the issue could still wind up in litigation.
More importantly, any proposition declared the winner is almost sure to face legal challenges on its own merits. Anticipating such lawsuits, Prop 40 includes a procedure for “expedited judicial review of this act.”
Here’s a brief look at the measures, and how they conflict.

Signs promote “yes” on Prop 40 and “no” on Props 41 and 42 before a rally at the Curran Theatre in San Francisco in early October.
Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle Proposition 40
Under Prop 40, most billionaires would owe a one-time 5% “excise” tax on net worth above $1.1 billion. The rate would be phased in between $1 billion and $1.1 billion.
The tax would apply to publicly traded securities, private-company stock, intellectual property and physical assets such as cars and artwork.
It would exclude homes, buildings and other real estate held directly by the taxpayer, as well as most retirement accounts. One exception: Roth IRA balances above $10 million would be taxed. Physical assets located outside California would also be excluded.

Article continues below this ad
The measure is sponsored by the Service Employees International Union — United Healthcare Workers West (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484470&session=2025&view=received).
The billionaire tax is what’s known as a “special tax,” in which tax revenues go toward a specific purpose rather than the state’s general fund. It stipulates that 90% of revenues would go toward Medi-Cal and other health coverage for lower-income people and the rest would go to public schools and food assistance. It’s meant to counteract the impending cuts from the Republican-led One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which was signed by President Donald Trump last year.
Prop 40 would exempt billionaire-tax revenues from constitutional requirements for education funding, budget reserves and the government-spending cap known as the Gann limit.
The Gann limit, passed by voters in 1979, restricts government spending from tax and fee revenues to 1978-79 levels, adjusted for changes in inflation and population. Anything over that limit must be refunded to taxpayers or spent on certain purposes, such as education.
Voters have approved many tax initiatives that exempted revenues from the Gann limit, such as the state gasoline, diesel fuel and cigarette taxes.
Proposition 41
Prop 41 has two provisions:
It would prohibit any state tax that is enacted or takes effect on or after Jan. 1, 2026, from the Gann limit, which experts widely agree would conflict with Prop 40.
The “obvious point” of this change, “hidden deep in the Proposition 41 text, is to nullify Proposition 40,” according to a paper co-authored (https://scholarship.law.missouri.edu/facpubs/1384/) by the drafters of Prop 40. “California’s fiscal rules are so complex, the only way to do fiscal policy anymore … is to waive the existing rules,” said Brian Galle, a UC Berkeley law professor and one of the authors.
It would impose new audit requirements on programs that receive revenues from special taxes.
For any special tax initiative, meaning one placed on the ballot by citizens, the state auditor would have to conduct a detailed “preelection financial and performance audit” of programs potentially getting funds once the initiative reached 25% of required signatures. An audit summary would appear on the ballot.
For all special taxes enacted by initiative or the Legislature on or after Jan. 1, 2026, the state auditor would have to conduct a financial and performance review every four years.
These audit provisions do not conflict with Prop 40, Kaye said. He contends that if Prop 40 and 41 both pass, the audit provisions “would stand regardless of how many votes Prop 40 gets.”
Not so fast, said Darien Shanske, a UC Davis law professor and co-drafter of Prop 40. “There would be a fight about that, of course,” but he does not think those provisions would survive on their own.
Proposition 42
Prop 42, the “Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026,” would prohibit wealth taxes (on anyone, not just billionaires) and retroactive taxes. Specifically:
It would prohibit any tax enacted on or after Jan. 1, 2026, on the “ownership or control” of personal property, which includes most assets other than real estate. The ban would include taxes on savings and other financial assets — whether they are inside or outside of retirement accounts — and physical possessions. It would apply to residents regardless of their net worth.
This provision would not apply to income or capital gains from investments, which the state already taxes, nor to the taxation of real estate.
It would bar taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, that apply retroactively, including ones based on a taxpayer’s residency status.
Props 41 and 42 were created and submitted by Building a Better California (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767&view=late1), whose major donors (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-spending-22463286.php) include Google co-founder Sergey Brin and a host of prominent CEOs, venture capitalists and other wealthy individuals. The same group is funding the opposition to Prop 40.
In their paper, the drafters of Prop 40 warn that the two competing measures “are poorly drafted in a manner that could pose serious threats to California’s fiscal future, with the potential to undermine key spending programs and potentially cause or worsen future budget crises.”
Molly Weedn, a spokesperson for Prop. 41, said via email, “Californians deserve more accountability and transparency for their hard earned tax dollars, and that is exactly what Prop 41 will offer.”
What if all three measures fail?
This is the most straightforward outcome: Nothing happens. Historically, it is also the most likely result.
Since 1912, California voters have approved 141 initiatives and rejected 256, for a success rate of 35%, according to California’s secretary of state.
Competing propositions have become “increasingly common” in recent decades, said Fredric Woocher, an attorney with Stumwasser and Woocher who specializes in election law. “It is becoming an effective technique to confuse voters and defeat measures that special interests don’t want passed.”
What does history show on conflicting props?
When voters face two conflicting ballot measures, “if they are really presented as competing alternatives, you don’t usually get them both winning,” Woocher said. “Usually you say, I will vote for one but not the other.” Or if they’re confused, they vote against both.
In November 1988, California voters faced five competing insurance measures, Props 100 through 104. Prop 103 (https://consumerwatchdog.org/insurance/insurance-reform-california-1988-insurance-wars/), sponsored by consumer groups, was the only one that got more than 50% and became law.
Legal experts believe the first time two conflicting initiatives won was in June 1988. Props 68 and 73 both dealt with campaign finance reform and got 53% and 58% of the vote, respectively. Prop 73 was declared the winner.
At first, the Fair Political Practices Commission, which was in charge of implementing the law, found a few parts of Prop 68 that did not directly conflict with Prop 73 and found them to be valid and enforceable.
But the commission was sued over that decision and in 1990, the California Supreme Court ruled against it. The court said: (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/3d/51/744.html) “When two or more measures are competing initiatives, either because they are expressly offered as ‘all-or-nothing’ alternatives or because each creates a comprehensive regulatory scheme related to the same subject … only the provisions of the measure receiving the highest number of affirmative votes (can) be enforced.”
(Meanwhile, the key parts of Prop 73 were later invalidated on grounds unrelated to Prop 68.)
Props 40, 41 and 42 all say that if this measure receives more “yes” votes than a measure deemed to be in conflict, this measure’s provisions “shall prevail in their entirety.” Props 41 and 42 then say that “all the provisions” of the other measure “shall be null and void” while Prop 40 only says that “any conflicting provisions of the other measure or measures shall be null and void.”
Nevertheless, if two competing measures pass in November, the losing side will probably argue that all or part of it should take effect.
For example, Prop 42 spokesman Nathan Click told the Chronicle via text that “if both 40 and 42 pass and 40 gets more votes, Prop 42 will not apply to the temporary (billionaire) tax, but it will apply to future taxes on personal property and personal savings.”
Galle, the co-author of Prop 40, responded that “courts will likely have to resolve some of these potential complications.”
Woocher said he thinks the courts will look at how the propositions were presented to voters. “If they are presented in the ballot arguments and campaign as ‘vote for these and not those,’ then that is significant evidence that the measure that got the most votes wins in its entirety and none of the other measures take effect.”

Prop 40 guide: Why ‘yes’ or ‘no’ depends on two other California propositions
By Kathleen Pender (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/kathleen-pender/) , Contributor Updated Oct 31, 2026 1:33 p.m.
From left, California insurance commissioner candidate Jane Kim, Sen. Bernie Sanders, independent-Vt., and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., stand together onstage after the “Ballots Over Billionaires” wealth tax rally at the Curran Theatre in San Francisco.
Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle
Many Californians have strong opinions about Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php), the proposed “wealth tax” on billionaires. But voting for — or against — this high-stakes ballot measure in November is not as simple as voting for — or against — Prop 40.
That’s because Props 41 and 42, which never mention billionaires but are backed by some of the state’s wealthiest residents, are also on the ballot and have provisions that conflict with Prop 40. (Props 41 and 42 do not conflict with each other.)

Under the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-10/), if two conflicting measures on the same ballot both pass with more than 50% of the vote, the one that gets the most “yes” votes prevails.
The graphic below shows the possible outcomes for which propositions could take effect, depending on how the votes come in. Voters can also use it to understand the cumulative impact of how they vote on each proposition.
What it means to vote ‘yes’ or ‘no’ on Props 40, 41 and 42
Prop 40, the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, would impose a one-time “wealth tax” on the net worth of people who were California residents as of Jan. 1, 2026 — even if they later became non-residents — and had more than $1 billion in net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. It also would exempt billionaire-tax revenues from three state-spending rules, including one known as the Gann limit.

Prop 41 would conflict with Prop 40 because it would outlaw new taxes passed after Jan. 1, 2026 that are exempt from the Gann limit. Prop 42 also appears to counter Prop 40 by preventing new taxes on personal property (i.e., wealth) and taxes that apply retroactively, including those based on residency.
Backers of the billionaire tax are urging people (https://yeson40.com/) to vote “Yes” on 40 and “No” on Props 41 and 42. If voters follow that advice or, vote the exact opposite way, the outcomes would be straightforward:
If Prop 40 passes with more than 50% of the vote and Prop 41 and Prop 42 do not: The billionaire tax would take effect and the other two would not.
If Prop 40 loses and Prop 41 and/or 42 pass: The billionaire tax would fail. Prop 41 would take effect if it got a simple majority. So would Prop 42 if it passed.
But what happens if Prop 40 gets more than half the vote, and so does Prop 41 and/or 42? Here is the conventional wisdom:

Prop 41 passes with more votes than Prop 40: Prop 41 takes effect and the billionaire does not.
Prop 42 passes with more votes than Prop 40: Prop 42 takes effect, the billionaire tax dies.
Prop 40 passes with more votes than Prop 41: Prop 40 gets enacted, Prop 41 is invalidated.
Prop 40 passes with more votes than Prop 42: Prop 40 takes effect, and cancels out Prop 42.
Although these are likely scenarios, anything could happen in a court of law. The losing side could argue that its proposition doesn’t conflict with the winning one, so they should both take effect. A court would have to decide if they do conflict.
The losing side also might argue that some parts of its measure do not conflict with the winning proposition — and those parts should take effect. The California Supreme Court has rejected this piecemeal approach, but the issue could still wind up in litigation.
More importantly, any proposition declared the winner is almost sure to face legal challenges on its own merits. Anticipating such lawsuits, Prop 40 includes a procedure for “expedited judicial review of this act.”
Here’s a brief look at the measures, and how they conflict.

Signs promote “yes” on Prop 40 and “no” on Props 41 and 42 before a rally at the Curran Theatre in San Francisco in early October.
Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle Proposition 40
Under Prop 40, most billionaires would owe a one-time 5% “excise” tax on net worth above $1.1 billion. The rate would be phased in between $1 billion and $1.1 billion.
The tax would apply to publicly traded securities, private-company stock, intellectual property and physical assets such as cars and artwork.
It would exclude homes, buildings and other real estate held directly by the taxpayer, as well as most retirement accounts. One exception: Roth IRA balances above $10 million would be taxed. Physical assets located outside California would also be excluded.

The measure is sponsored by the Service Employees International Union — United Healthcare Workers West (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484470&session=2025&view=received).
The billionaire tax is what’s known as a “special tax,” in which tax revenues go toward a specific purpose rather than the state’s general fund. It stipulates that 90% of revenues would go toward Medi-Cal and other health coverage for lower-income people and the rest would go to public schools and food assistance. It’s meant to counteract the impending cuts from the Republican-led One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which was signed by President Donald Trump last year.
Prop 40 would exempt billionaire-tax revenues from constitutional requirements for education funding, budget reserves and the government-spending cap known as the Gann limit.
The Gann limit, passed by voters in 1979, restricts government spending from tax and fee revenues to 1978-79 levels, adjusted for changes in inflation and population. Anything over that limit must be refunded to taxpayers or spent on certain purposes, such as education.
Voters have approved many tax initiatives that exempted revenues from the Gann limit, such as the state gasoline, diesel fuel and cigarette taxes.
Proposition 41
Prop 41 has two provisions:
It would prohibit any state tax that is enacted or takes effect on or after Jan. 1, 2026, from the Gann limit, which experts widely agree would conflict with Prop 40.
The “obvious point” of this change, “hidden deep in the Proposition 41 text, is to nullify Proposition 40,” according to a paper co-authored (https://scholarship.law.missouri.edu/facpubs/1384/) by the drafters of Prop 40. “California’s fiscal rules are so complex, the only way to do fiscal policy anymore … is to waive the existing rules,” said Brian Galle, a UC Berkeley law professor and one of the authors.
It would impose new audit requirements on programs that receive revenues from special taxes.
For any special tax initiative, meaning one placed on the ballot by citizens, the state auditor would have to conduct a detailed “preelection financial and performance audit” of programs potentially getting funds once the initiative reached 25% of required signatures. An audit summary would appear on the ballot.
For all special taxes enacted by initiative or the Legislature on or after Jan. 1, 2026, the state auditor would have to conduct a financial and performance review every four years.
These audit provisions do not conflict with Prop 40, Kaye said. He contends that if Prop 40 and 41 both pass, the audit provisions “would stand regardless of how many votes Prop 40 gets.”
Not so fast, said Darien Shanske, a UC Davis law professor and co-drafter of Prop 40. “There would be a fight about that, of course,” but he does not think those provisions would survive on their own.
Proposition 42
Prop 42, the “Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026,” would prohibit wealth taxes (on anyone, not just billionaires) and retroactive taxes. Specifically:
It would prohibit any tax enacted on or after Jan. 1, 2026, on the “ownership or control” of personal property, which includes most assets other than real estate. The ban would include taxes on savings and other financial assets — whether they are inside or outside of retirement accounts — and physical possessions. It would apply to residents regardless of their net worth.
This provision would not apply to income or capital gains from investments, which the state already taxes, nor to the taxation of real estate.
It would bar taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, that apply retroactively, including ones based on a taxpayer’s residency status.
Props 41 and 42 were created and submitted by Building a Better California (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767&view=late1), whose major donors (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-spending-22463286.php) include Google co-founder Sergey Brin and a host of prominent CEOs, venture capitalists and other wealthy individuals. The same group is funding the opposition to Prop 40.
In their paper, the drafters of Prop 40 warn that the two competing measures “are poorly drafted in a manner that could pose serious threats to California’s fiscal future, with the potential to undermine key spending programs and potentially cause or worsen future budget crises.”
Molly Weedn, a spokesperson for Prop. 41, said via email, “Californians deserve more accountability and transparency for their hard earned tax dollars, and that is exactly what Prop 41 will offer.”
What if all three measures fail?
This is the most straightforward outcome: Nothing happens. Historically, it is also the most likely result.
Since 1912, California voters have approved 141 initiatives and rejected 256, for a success rate of 35%, according to California’s secretary of state.
Competing propositions have become “increasingly common” in recent decades, said Fredric Woocher, an attorney with Stumwasser and Woocher who specializes in election law. “It is becoming an effective technique to confuse voters and defeat measures that special interests don’t want passed.”
What does history show on conflicting props?
When voters face two conflicting ballot measures, “if they are really presented as competing alternatives, you don’t usually get them both winning,” Woocher said. “Usually you say, I will vote for one but not the other.” Or if they’re confused, they vote against both.
In November 1988, California voters faced five competing insurance measures, Props 100 through 104. Prop 103 (https://consumerwatchdog.org/insurance/insurance-reform-california-1988-insurance-wars/), sponsored by consumer groups, was the only one that got more than 50% and became law.
Legal experts believe the first time two conflicting initiatives won was in June 1988. Props 68 and 73 both dealt with campaign finance reform and got 53% and 58% of the vote, respectively. Prop 73 was declared the winner.
At first, the Fair Political Practices Commission, which was in charge of implementing the law, found a few parts of Prop 68 that did not directly conflict with Prop 73 and found them to be valid and enforceable.
But the commission was sued over that decision and in 1990, the California Supreme Court ruled against it. The court said: (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/3d/51/744.html) “When two or more measures are competing initiatives, either because they are expressly offered as ‘all-or-nothing’ alternatives or because each creates a comprehensive regulatory scheme related to the same subject … only the provisions of the measure receiving the highest number of affirmative votes (can) be enforced.”
(Meanwhile, the key parts of Prop 73 were later invalidated on grounds unrelated to Prop 68.)
Props 40, 41 and 42 all say that if this measure receives more “yes” votes than a measure deemed to be in conflict, this measure’s provisions “shall prevail in their entirety.” Props 41 and 42 then say that “all the provisions” of the other measure “shall be null and void” while Prop 40 only says that “any conflicting provisions of the other measure or measures shall be null and void.”
Nevertheless, if two competing measures pass in November, the losing side will probably argue that all or part of it should take effect.
For example, Prop 42 spokesman Nathan Click told the Chronicle via text that “if both 40 and 42 pass and 40 gets more votes, Prop 42 will not apply to the temporary (billionaire) tax, but it will apply to future taxes on personal property and personal savings.”
Galle, the co-author of Prop 40, responded that “courts will likely have to resolve some of these potential complications.”
Woocher said he thinks the courts will look at how the propositions were presented to voters. “If they are presented in the ballot arguments and campaign as ‘vote for these and not those,’ then that is significant evidence that the measure that got the most votes wins in its entirety and none of the other measures take effect.”

PROP 41: Special-Tax Audits and the Spending-Limit Lock
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2041.pdf)
Research

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Summary
Proposition 41 would write two rules into the California Constitution. First, programs funded by new state special taxes would face independent audits by the state auditor. These audits would occur when the ballot initiative is initially proposed and then every four years after a special tax takes effect. Second, no new state tax could circumvent the Gann limit, the voter-approved spending cap adopted in 1979. Hoover Institution research shows that California’s spending has grown far faster than inflation or population and that the state budget rises and falls with the fortunes of a small number of high-income taxpayers. Proposition 41 is best read as an attempt to restore discipline to that budget. It also contains a clause that, if it outpolls Proposition 40, would void the billionaire tax on the same ballot (see California Decides, Prop 40: The Billionaire Tax Act (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-40)).
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues from State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”
Measure’s own name: The Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0040A1).
Type: Initiated constitutional amendment.
A vote YES means: Starting retroactively on January 1, 2026, any program that would be the recipient of new or increased special tax revenues as a result of a citizen initiative must undergo state performance audits prior to the vote. Such programs, and those receiving revenues from legislatively enacted new or increased special taxes, must be audited every four years thereafter. No new state tax or increase to a state tax enacted on or after that date may route its revenue outside California’s voter-approved spending limit, commonly referred to as the Gann limit.
A vote NO means: California keeps current law. New special taxes are not subject to this audit regime, and new taxes may continue to direct revenue into funds that sit outside the Gann limit, as several existing taxes already do.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0040A1, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0040A1%20(Gov.%20Efficiency).pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 25-0040 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-040)
1. Overview
Proposition 41 would add a new Article XXIV, titled “Protecting Taxpayer Dollars,” to the California Constitution. It has two main provisions.
The first provision is an audit requirement for programs that would receive funds from proposed special tax initiatives. A special tax is one whose revenue is dedicated to specific purposes rather than available for general use. When the proponents of a citizen initiative that would create a new or increased special tax notify the secretary of state that they have gathered 25 percent of the required signatures, the state auditor must begin a financial and performance audit of each program the special tax would fund. The audit must assess program effectiveness, evaluate the potential for fraud, waste, and abuse, and recommend ways the program could achieve budgetary savings of at least 10 percent a year. If the measure qualifies for the ballot, an executive summary of the audit must be printed in the state voter information guide.
A subsequent audit must be repeated every four years for every new or increased special tax enacted by the legislature or by voters on or after January 1, 2026. When a tax passes, the audit costs are reimbursed from the tax’s own revenue. When a tax initiative fails to qualify or is rejected, the general fund absorbs the cost.
The second provision protects the state spending limit from being circumvented by future state taxes. The Gann limit, adopted by voters as Proposition 4 in 1979 and amended by Proposition 111 in 1990, caps how much tax revenue the state may appropriate each year. It’s adjusted for increases to population and per capita income, and some substantial categories of spending are excluded from the cap. According to the Gann limit, if tax revenue exceeds the limit over two consecutive years the excess revenue must be split between taxpayer rebates and additional K–14 school funding. For context, rapid tax revenue growth has rarely resulted in mandatory Gann limit rebates.
However, under current rules a new tax can be written to deposit its revenue in a fund that is excluded from the appropriations counted against the Gann limit. Proposition 41 would forbid that design for any state tax enacted by the legislature or by voter initiative, but the ban is limited to taxes that take effect on or after January 1, 2026. New special taxes would still be permitted, but their revenue would simply count toward the same spending cap that applies to other nonexempt tax revenues.
The second provision connects Proposition 41 to Proposition 40, the Billionaire Tax Act. If Prop 40 is approved it would route its revenue into a separate reserve fund that sits outside the structure of the Gann limit, the Proposition 98 school-funding guarantee, and the rainy-day budget rules. Proposition 41 prohibits new or increased state taxes from circumventing the structure intended to limit the growth of California government spending, and it includes specific text that will nullify Proposition 40 if both initiatives pass but Proposition 41 receives more yes votes.
2. The legal language
Full text:
Initiative 25-0040A1, “The Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0040A1%20(Gov.%20Efficiency).pdf) (eight pages, amended language submitted January 12, 2026).
Key language:
“No state tax that is enacted or takes effect on or after January 1, 2026 shall be exempted or excluded from the Government Spending Limitation. The State of California shall not impose, collect, or enforce any state tax that is enacted or takes effect on or after January 1, 2026 if the state tax is exempted or excluded from the Government Spending Limitation.”
What it amends: Adds a new Article XXIV, titled “Protecting Taxpayer Dollars,” to the California Constitution. The article defines “Government Spending Limitation” as Article XIII B, the Gann limit, and defines an exempted tax as one whose revenue is deposited outside the general fund and left out of the appropriations subject to the limit or that raises the appropriations limit by statute.
Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it. The measure also includes a self-defense provision that appoints and funds independent counsel through a continuous general fund appropriation if the governor and attorney general decline to defend it.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
What?
It would create constitutionally required audits of programs funded by new or increased special taxes, both before a tax initiative reaches voters and every four years after a tax takes effect. It also creates a ban on excluding the revenue from any new or increased state tax from the Gann spending limit.
Where?
Statewide, written into the California Constitution.
When?
It takes effect on passage and reaches back to taxes enacted or effective on or after January 1, 2026.
Why?
The initiative’s authors frame it as a response to California’s nation-leading tax rates and their effect on the state’s affordability crisis. The stated purpose is to require up-front, recurring audits of programs funded by special taxes and to prevent new taxes from circumventing the Gann limit so that surplus revenue is refunded rather than spent.
4. Analysis and Assessment
Audit requirements of Proposition 41 address a documented problem. For example, in 2024 the state auditor found that California spent roughly $24 billion on homelessness and housing programs over five fiscal years without consistently tracking whether the money reduced homelessness. Three of the five programs reviewed did not produce enough data to judge their cost-effectiveness at all. Proposition 41 would make that kind of review routine for programs funded by new special taxes, and it would give voters an audit summary before they vote on a tax initiative. Independent, recurring performance audits with concrete savings targets are the kind of accountability that good-government advocates across the spectrum have long sought.
Proposition 41’s requirement that future special taxes be subject to the Gann limit is similarly reasonable: California’s fiscal challenge is accelerated spending, not a shortage of revenue. Research by Hoover Institution Senior Fellow Lee Ohanian shows that from 2019 to 2023 California’s population fell by almost 500,000 people, while the state budget grew nearly 57 percent (31 percent after inflation). Additional research by Hoover fellows Lanhee J. Chen and Joshua D. Rauh describes how California’s heavy reliance on the personal income tax, which now supplies most general fund tax revenue, ties the budget to the performance of the stock market. In 2021, the top 10 percent of taxpayers paid almost 90 percent of personal income tax revenue. Meanwhile, the state budget swung $175 billion from a surplus in 2022 to a deficit in 2024.
The Gann limit is one of the few constitutional tools that restrains government spending growth during economic booms that becomes a fiscal catastrophe during leaner times. Prior analysis by Hoover Fellow Bill Whalen has traced how the Gann limit’s fiscal discipline has been eroded over time, from Proposition 111’s 1990 exclusion of new gas tax revenue to budgeting practices that kept billions out of the limit calculation. Proposition 41 would close the special-fund circumvention for any future tax.
Importantly, Prop 41 does not ban new taxes, nor does it cut existing programs. It simply requires that revenue from any new tax be counted alongside the rest of state spending, so that a future surplus is dedicated to a tax rebate and additional school funding (per Prop 4 and Prop 111) rather than accumulating in a dedicated fund. This rule should help encourage policymakers to be more thoughtful about expanding government programs when tax revenues unexpectedly increase.
Like Proposition 42, Proposition 41 contains a clause that, if it outpolls Proposition 40, would nullify Prop 40. This specificity is likely preferable to asking the courts to decide which parts of two conflicting constitutional amendments survive.
5. Conclusion
Proposition 41 would require any programs receiving funding from new or increased special taxes to be audited by the state auditor to assess performance, evaluate potential for waste, fraud, and abuse, and identify explicit cost savings opportunities. It would also require each new state tax enacted by the legislature or by voter initiative to be subject to the Gann limit. Its most immediate effect would be to nullify Proposition 40 if it draws more yes votes, while its lasting effect would be to hold all future state taxes to the same spending cap as the rest of the budget.
Hoover Institution research shows that California’s fiscal problem is driven by spending increases that have managed to outstrip even the state’s strong tax revenue growth. From that perspective, Proposition 41 would offer increased oversight on how well California is spending taxpayer dollars.

Proposition 41: Audits For New State Special Taxes
Proposition 41: Audits For New State Special Taxes
Proposition 41: Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits For New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Tax Audits, One-Time Wealth Tax for State-Funded Health Care Programs Initiative.
Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026
The Transparency Act
Summary
Proposition 41 was placed on the ballot by petition signatures to amend the California Constitution. It began as Initiative #25-0041A (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0040A1%20%28Gov.%20Efficiency%29.pdf) , filed with the California Attorney General’s Office. Prop. 41 amends the California Constitution by adding Article XXIV, creating audit review requirements for special tax measures and enforcing state appropriation limits (the Gann Limit) for all future state tax measures.
Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to conduct a financial and performance audit of any citizen initiative proposing a new special tax once the campaign collects 25% of required signatures. The auditor must review specific criteria set by Proposition 41, including identifying ways to cut the proposed program’s annual costs by 10%. If the measure qualifies, an executive summary of the audit is published in the official voter information pamphlet.
Additionally, the State Auditor will conduct ongoing audits every four years for programs receiving funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or voters after January 1, 2026.
Proposition 41 specifies that the costs of these audits will be reimbursed using revenue generated from the new tax if voters approve the measure. If a special tax initiative fails, the state general fund covers the audit costs.
It would also prohibit the state from enforcing any new tax enacted or effective on or after January 1, 2026, that is exempted or excluded from the state spending limit.
Proposition 41 conflicts directly with Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm) (the Billionaire Wealth Tax initiative). If both pass, whichever measure receives more "yes" votes will prevail in its entirety. Because Proposition 40 excludes its revenues from the state spending limit, Proposition 41 would render Proposition 40 unenforceable if Proposition 41 wins more votes.
Note about the Gann Limit: Approved by California voters in 1979 asProposition 4 (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/ca_ballot_props/864/), the Gann Limit restricts how much tax revenue state and local governments (including school districts) can spend each year, adjusted annually for population changes and economic growth. The limit applies to both General Fund taxes (unrestricted funds for general government operations) and special taxes (funds earmarked for specific purposes), though certain spending categories—such as infrastructure and emergency response—are exempt. (Sources: California Budget Center, What is the Gann Limit? (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians) , Gann Limit (Wikipedia) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gann_Limit) , CA Department of Finance, Description of (https://dof.ca.gov/media/docs/budget/california-budget-frequently-asked-questions/fundclassifications.pdf)Fund Classifications in the Treasury (https://dof.ca.gov/media/docs/budget/california-budget-frequently-asked-questions/fundclassifications.pdf))
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. However, the State Auditor costs will increase due to the new and ongoing work to carry out the audit requirements in this measure.
Due to additional pages of audit information being included in the voter information guides could increase state printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative on the ballot.
What your vote means (LAO Analysis)
YES: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.

Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 41 improves transparency and reduces government waste by requiring independent state audits of programs funded by new special taxes while ensuring all state taxes respect voter-approved spending caps, as detailed in the Official Voter Information Guide.
Opponents contend that the measure was put on the ballot by billionaire opponents to block Prop. 40, a proposed wealth tax on billionaires, and that its audit requirements create unnecessary hurdles to funding essential public services like healthcare and education.

Proposition 41
Require audits of new tax programs
This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters. The auditor would assess whether the program that would receive funding could cut spending by at least 10% annually. Any new special tax approved by voters would count toward California’s spending limit, potentially triggering automatic refunds that reduce funding for other state programs. If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes. It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the proposed billionaire tax.

Supporters say key social programs are not getting enough funding despite California’s high taxes. They argue the state auditor should assess whether the programs that would benefit from special taxes are spending money wisely. Supporters also want these special taxes to count toward the state spending limit, making tax rebates to Californians more likely.
Oppose
The chief opponent is SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the sponsor of Proposition 40. The union argues that Prop. 41 is designed to trick voters into unknowingly blocking a wealth tax on billionaires. Prop. 41 isn’t about auditing waste in public programs, the union says; instead it’s a way for billionaires to avoid paying taxes once on their huge wealth.

Endorsement: Prop 41 is a cynical poison pill. And it isn’t the only one on California’s ballot
Prop 41 is one of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
It wouldn’t be a California election without a few petty, revenge-motivated ballot measures.
Proposition 41 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop41-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is one of two poison pill attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax. The measure explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 41 or its cousin initiative Prop 42 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-proposition-42-taxes-22449389.php) pass with a larger number of votes.
Backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php), Prop 41 would require new special taxes that raise money for specific purposes to adhere to state spending rules, while mandating regular audits of the programs they fund.
What’s so bad about ensuring California spends tax revenue wisely?

Well, nothing — if that’s what the measure actually does. But it’s a cheap ruse to nullify Prop 40.
The measure targets an obscure — but extremely consequential — spending rule embedded in California’s Constitution.
Known as the Gann Limit (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4416), that rule prevents the state from spending more money per taxpayer than it did in 1979 — the year voters approved the measure — once adjusted for inflation. Any money the state collects over the limit must be either refunded to taxpayers or spent on certain purposes, such as infrastructure or education.

Article continues below this ad
Prop 41 would prohibit any state tax taking effect on or after Jan. 1, 2026 from sidestepping those requirements. That would neuter Prop 40, which explicitly exempts its one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires from the Gann Limit to backfill federal healthcare cuts.
Loren Kaye, former president of a California Chamber of Commerce-affiliated think tank and a Prop 41 supporter, told us in an endorsement interview that the measure establishes a “level playing field so that everybody is similarly affected once you reach the limit.”
We agree that budget carveouts generally aren’t a good idea. But the Gann Limit isn’t sacrosanct; there are perfectly legitimate reasons for excluding certain revenues from its rules.
Consider California’s Hospital Quality Assurance Fee Program (https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/providers-partners/hospital-quality-assurance-fee-program-hqaf/), which charges hospitals a fee to unlock matching federal healthcare funds and improve services for low-income patients. These funds are currently exempt from the Gann Limit (https://funds.dof.ca.gov/app/download/3158) — a provision voters approved when they green-lighted Prop 52 in 2016 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=52&year=2016).
But the federal government, which has to approve the tax, could easily demand changes to its structure. If that were to happen and Prop 41 passes, the hospital fee program could arguably be considered a “new” special tax — and thus be subject to the Gann Limit, diverting money away from hospitals, argued David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent.

California’s financial regulations are impossibly complex after decades of ballot-box budgeting. Adding another restriction is only bound to make things worse.
Meanwhile, Prop 41’s audit requirements are, as Darien Shanske, a UC Davis School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent, put it, meant to be “the chocolate coating that’s supposed to attract people.”
But they’re largely redundant and would decrease efficiency.
Prop 41 requires the state auditor to evaluate programs that will receive funding from new citizen-proposed special taxes and include its findings in the official voter information guide. But the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office already assesses each ballot initiative’s fiscal and practical impact (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop41-110326.pdf) — including at the 25% signature-gathering threshold Prop 41 identifies — and those analyses are included in the voter guide.
The measure’s ongoing audit requirement could also be counterproductive; tax measures typically contain accountability provisions, and adding an untold number of audits to the already overworked auditor’s office could distract from other critical investigations. Furthermore, Prop 41 directs the state auditor’s office to find 10% annual savings in program costs, which is arbitrary and dilutes the office’s independence.

By Editorial Board | editorial@santacruzsentinel.com (mailto:editorial@santacruzsentinel.com) | Santa Cruz Sentinel
PUBLISHED: October 22, 2026 at 3:52 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
No measure on the Nov. 3 ballot has drawn more attention than Proposition 40, the “billionaires’ tax.”
As the measure drew early support, it wasn’t difficult to figure out why: Who in truth really likes or trusts billionaires?
But the history of wealth taxes is they raise far less revenue than hoped for, because wealthy taxpayers find ways to avoid them.
The SEIU United Healthcare Workers West and like-minded allies are selling Prop. 40 as a “one-time” 5% tax on the wealth of residents with more than $1 billion in net worth. They claim the tax will raise $100 billion from 200 billionaires.
But wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists. According to a new report from the conservative Hoover Institution’s Joshua Rauh and Benjamin Jaro the tax would actually result in a net revenue loss of $38.9 billion for the state.
And the losses have already begun as seven billionaires with $539.9 billion in wealth moved out of California between Prop. 40’s filing last autumn and the date at which residency would be determined for purposes of assessing the tax (Jan. 1, 2026).
And that means nearly 30% of Prop. 40’s estimated $1.9 trillion potential tax base has already disappeared. And it’s plausible that other billionaires have subsequently left the state or could otherwise avoid the tax, since the economists identify at least eight Prop. 40 legal vulnerabilities, including its assessment of a taxpayer’s worldwide assets and dubious valuation methods for non-publicly traded assets.
Even if only some of Prop. 40’s provisions are struck down, such an outcome would further shrink the tax base.
And there’s more potential losses as California will also lose annual income tax payments from billionaires who leave, with estimates billionaires pay between $3.3 billion and $5.8 billion annually in state income tax.
What makes Proposition 40 dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the past two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes. Absent Prop. 40, these income-tax payments would grow with incomes. The Hoover economists estimate these reduced payments would exceed wealth tax revenue.
For all those reasons, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs, with any gains likely to be temporary.
The SEIU created Prop. 40 to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their friends. Opposition to this measure includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
Prop. 40 has already done damage, and if it passes, expect more pain than gain. Vote No on Prop. 40.
Propositions 41 and 42
To counter Prop. 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaire tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future.
Prop. 41 would mandate that the state auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as audit ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Prop. 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago.
We’re not living in the 1970s. The state needs flexibility to address issues voters of that era never had to deal with — six-figure college costs, seven-figure mortgages and 13-figure wildfire costs.
Prop. 42 would prohibit the state from taxing retroactively. And it would permanently ban the state from any new taxes on ownership of financial assets or other personal properties — stocks, bonds, intellectual property, artwork, etc.
Taxes on wealth, however, are rarely ideal, and our opposition to Prop. 40 reflects that.
Prop. 42 was written by the AI boom’s beneficiaries, who are now among the wealthiest humans in history as part of an explosion of inequality, and the unpredictable course of AI’s development could well extend the huge gap between the haves and have-nots.
If this initiative had limited itself to nullifying Prop. 40, we could have supported it. However, California must not surrender its future freedom of action to defeat a single, one-time tax proposal.
Reject Propositions 40, 41 and 42.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 5:03 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:07 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes. Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting “yes” would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they’re on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.
Related Articles
We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting “yes” could also mean that Proposition 40 (the “billionaire tax”), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop. 41.
Voting “no” would mean that the state auditor’s role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes. More information for the voters.
Generally, opponents don’t like the extra restrictions on how voter-approved tax money is raised and spent and how the programs meant to be funded could be weakened or stalled. They also suggest that Props. 41 and 42 were heavily supported by billionaires in order to defeat Prop. 40.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem is Prop. 41 solving?
State spending is up 79% since 2019. Every year, billions of taxpayer dollars flow into state programs, like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned tax money we pay to the state.
While this is a city wide example, it’s exactly the kind of reason why we need audits and transparent accountability before it’s too late to put programs back on track: Audit: San Jose failed to adequately track $300 million in homelessness spending (https://www.mercurynews.com/2024/04/13/audit-san-jose-failed-to-adequately-track-300-million-in-homelessness-spending/).
Why is this the best solution to the problem?
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by new special tax measures, with the results posted publicly in the state Voter Information Guide.
This ensures voters have detailed information about the programs they’re being asked to raise taxes to fund.
If taxes are approved, Prop. 41 also requires ongoing public audits of the programs funded by those taxes to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals and recommend improvements.
It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit — so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Why is it necessary to audit a tax proposal before it even officially qualifies for the ballot?
Providing pre-ballot information about proposed initiatives is very typical. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) and the attorney general are required by state law to provide pre-ballot information on every measure that is filed.
Prop. 41 is actually much narrower — the auditor only commences with an audit once a measure collects 25% of the signatures needed to qualify for the ballot; and it only applies to initiatives that increase taxes.
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct pre-election financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new state special taxes. The state auditor’s findings must be shared widely with the public, including in the state’s official Voter Information Guide.
This pre-election audit will give voters clear, unbiased information on the programs a proposed tax would support. These audits are more extensive than any existing information provided to voters. This fills in a critical gap in the information provided to voters. The current initiative analyses from the LAO are required by law to provide only a description of the measure. Alternatively, under Prop. 41 the auditor will also provide voters a performance evaluation of programs funded by new taxes.
If a proposed tax fails to make the ballot, the state’s general fund still has to pay for the audit. Why should taxpayers foot the bill for failed political ideas?
The value to voters in seeing this detailed information about programs before they’re asked to vote far outweighs the marginal cost of conducting the audit and printing it in the Voter Guide.
Again, this is very typical under the status quo. The LAO and the attorney general already have to provide a description and a title and summary for each and every initiative measure — including those that fail — and the General Fund pays for those costs. It is also important to recognize that the extra costs imposed on the General Fund by Prop. 41 are exceedingly small. The LAO found that Prop. 41 would impose only minimal costs upon the General Fund. Further, providing more impartial, expert information to voters when decided to approve higher taxes is money well spent.
This also fails to take into account Prop. 41’s upside. As the LAO noted in the Voter Guide, Prop. 41 would result in taxpayer savings or improved services by implementing the auditor’s recommendations.
Prop. 41 contains conflict provisions stating that if it receives more “yes” votes than a competing tax measure like Prop. 40 (the billionaire wealth tax), then Prop. 40 is nullified entirely. How do proponents respond to claims that Prop. 41 is merely a “poison pill” designed to defeat the wealth tax rather than a stand-alone oversight tool?
California has faced issues with ineffective and inefficient state spending for years: homelessness, state technology programs, EDD are just a few recent examples. Prop. 40 is just the latest proposal that would fuel ineffective spending.
Prop. 40 seeks to raise tens of billions of dollars in new tax revenue, but contains zero transparency, accountability or safeguards to ensure the money is spent as intended. For instance, Prop. 40 contains no safeguards to ensure that billions of dollars don’t flow to health insurance company profits and CEOs under the guise of “saving health care.”

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes. Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting “yes” would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they’re on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.
